title: Apollo lines up $75B in AI chip leases, dwarfing every neocloud
subtitle: Two separate financings — $35B of Google TPUs for Anthropic and $40B of Nvidia Vera Rubin chips for SpaceX — would give Apollo more AI compute under lease than CoreWeave, Valor, and the next three neoclouds combined.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Apollo Global Management is positioned to control roughly $75 billion in AI chips through two separate chip-leasing structures, according to new reporting this week. The Anthropic leg, announced in June, is a $35 billion financing arranged with Broadcom and Blackstone to buy Google Tensor Processing Units and lease them to Anthropic — processors delivered gradually starting in the first half of 2027. The SpaceX leg, disclosed in a recent SEC filing, is a roughly $40 billion deal in which a special purpose vehicle managed by Apollo-backed Atlas SP will purchase Nvidia Vera Rubin systems and rent them to SpaceX under a five-year agreement with no residual value guarantee.

The scale is the story. CoreWeave, the largest listed neocloud, has raised $27.2 billion in chip-backed financing since 2023. Valor, the next largest, has raised $5.4 billion. Apollo's two deals combined are nearly double every other chip-backed financier's running total. The structure also differs from a classic neocloud in a material way: Apollo is not building a compute business, it is originating asset-backed debt where the collateral is depreciating GPUs with lease-rate exposure to a handful of frontier labs. The entire thesis depends on those labs remaining able to meet lease payments through the end of the decade.

Two risks sit under the surface. First, the SpaceX leg routes compute to xAI and anchor sub-tenants — reportedly including Anthropic and Google themselves — with 90-day termination clauses. A short-notice unwind on an $8B/year payment stream is a liquidity hazard the SPV's debt stack has to absorb. Second, the Vera Rubin generation's useful life as frontier compute is the open question. If model-efficiency improvements compress the serving GPU curve — which is what several labs are now targeting for 2027–2028 — the residual value of a five-year-old rack of Vera Rubin cards in 2032 is meaningfully lower than the lease pricing currently assumes. Apollo's deal has no residual guarantee, which is to say the SPV eats that risk, not Nvidia.

A note for learners: finance has become the rate-limiting resource in frontier AI, more than chips, power, or talent. The labs that will compete at the frontier through 2030 are the ones that can secure multi-decade compute at predictable prices, which is why the structuring question — who holds the chip, who holds the risk, who holds the residual — matters as much as the model architecture. If you are early-career and curious about AI economics, learn how an asset-backed SPV works. The instrument that will shape which labs stay in the race is not a research paper, it is a lease covenant.
